problem: Session 28 deliberately left a gap: switching only delivers frames within a single broadcast domain, using MAC addresses that have no meaning beyond the local segment. But an enterprise isn't one segment — it's dozens or hundreds of subnets across floors, buildings, data centers, and cloud regions, and its users need to reach the public internet too. Something has to move traffic between these separate networks. That something is routing.

Without routing, every network you've ever used would be an isolated island. A FundedNext support agent's workstation on one subnet couldn't reach a database server on another subnet, let alone a payment processor's API on the public internet. Routing is what turns a collection of separate local networks into one interconnected "network of networks" — literally what the word internet means.
concept: Routing is the process of forwarding packets between different networks based on destination IP address, performed by a router (a Layer 3 device) using a routing table that maps destination networks to the next hop or exit interface to reach them. Where a switch asks "which port does this MAC address live on," a router asks "which network does this IP address belong to, and how do I get there."

Question Switching (Session 28) Routing (this session) Operates at Layer 2 (Data Link) Layer 3 (Network) Forwards based on Destination MAC address Destination IP address Scope Within one broadcast domain / subnet Between different networks/subnets Decision table MAC address table (CAM table) Routing table
deep: The routing table Every router (and every host, in a simpler form — see Session 24) maintains a routing table listing known destination networks, each with a next-hop address or exit interface, and a metric indicating preference when multiple routes exist. A router consults this table for every packet, using the longest prefix match (the most specific matching route wins) to decide where to send it next.

Field Meaning Destination network The network address and subnet mask this route applies to (e.g., 10.10.20.0/24) Next hop The IP address of the next router to forward toward, or the local interface if directly connected Metric / Administrative Distance A cost value used to pick the best route when multiple paths exist Interface Which physical/logical interface the packet should exit Directly connected vs. learned routes
Directly connected routes — networks the router has an interface physically/logically on; added automatically.
Static routes — manually configured by an administrator, pointing traffic for a specific network to a specific next hop.
Dynamic routes — learned automatically via a routing protocol (OSPF, EIGRP, BGP — previewed here, covered fully in Session 36) that lets routers exchange reachability information with each other.

The default route A default route (0.0.0.0/0 in IPv4) is the "catch-all" entry used when no more specific route matches a destination — typically pointing toward the internet-facing gateway. This is what lets an internal host reach any public IP address without the router needing an explicit entry for every network on the internet.

4. Internal Workflow — A Packet Crossing a Router Continuing the ongoing HTTPS example, at the moment a packet needs to leave the local subnet (destination IP is not on the same network as the sender):

1. The sending host compares the destination IP against its own subnet mask; determining it's off-subnet, it sends the frame to its default gateway's MAC address (resolved via ARP, Session 41) instead of the destination's MAC.
2. The router receives the frame, strips the Ethernet header (Layer 2 framing is discarded — it was only valid for that one hop), and examines the IP packet.
3. The router performs a routing table lookup using longest prefix match against the destination IP.

4. The router decrements the packet's TTL (Time To Live) by 1 — if TTL reaches 0, the packet is dropped and an ICMP Time Exceeded message is sent back (this is exactly how traceroute works, previewed here, detailed in Session 42).
5. The router rebuilds a brand-new Ethernet frame with its own MAC as the source and the next hop's MAC as the destination, then forwards it out the appropriate interface.

6. This process (steps 2–5) repeats at every router hop until the packet reaches a router directly connected to the destination network, which delivers the frame using ordinary switching to the final host.

The key insight: Ethernet framing is rebuilt at every single hop, while the IP packet itself (and its TTL) persists end- to-end — this is precisely why MAC addresses are described as local-only in Session 27, and IP addresses as globally significant.
enterprise: In enterprise design, routing happens at multiple points: distribution-layer or core-layer switches often perform inter- VLAN routing between departments on the same campus; dedicated edge routers connect the enterprise to ISPs and the public internet; and in the data center, routing connects application tiers, storage networks, and cloud interconnects. Routing tables and their associated routing protocols (Session 36) are frequently the single most business-critical configuration in an enterprise network — a routing misconfiguration can silently blackhole an entire site's traffic.

Session 27 (Ethernet) — routers rebuild Ethernet frames at every hop, so router behavior only makes sense with frame structure already understood.
Session 26 (TCP/IP Model) — routing is the concrete mechanism implementing the model's Internet layer.
Session 41 (ARP, upcoming) — hosts and routers both rely on ARP to resolve the next hop's MAC address before a frame can actually be sent.
Session 30 (Subnetting) and Sessions 31–32 (IPv4/IPv6) — the addressing scheme routing tables are built from.
Session 36 (Routing Protocols) — the automated, scalable version of the manual/static routing concepts introduced here.
Session 37 (NAT) — commonly performed at the same router boundary where routing decisions are made, especially at the internet edge.
Session 38 (ACL) — access control lists are frequently applied directly on router interfaces, filtering the same traffic routing decisions are made for.
security: Route hijacking / spoofing — a malicious or misconfigured router advertising false routes can redirect traffic through an attacker-controlled path (a serious concern at internet scale with BGP, previewed in Session 36).

Routers are natural chokepoints for security controls — ACLs (Session 38) and firewall rules are frequently applied at router interfaces because all inter-network traffic must pass through them by definition.
A misconfigured or overly permissive default route can inadvertently expose internal networks to unwanted paths — reviewing routing tables is a standard part of network security audits.

TTL-based traceroute behavior (used to map network paths, previewed above) can also be used maliciously for network reconnaissance, which is one reason some enterprises rate-limit or filter ICMP Time Exceeded responses at their perimeter.
troubleshooting: Symptom Likely Cause Check Can reach local subnet but nothing beyond it Missing/wrong default gateway, gateway down ipconfig/ip route, ping gateway Some remote networks reachable, others not Missing or incorrect specific route entry show ip route, traceroute to isolate the failing hop Traffic reaches destination but replies don't return Asymmetric routing, missing return route traceroute in both directions if possible Intermittent reachability to a specific network Flapping route, redundant path instability show ip route repeatedly, check routing protocol logs Windows: tracert 8.8.8.8 Linux: traceroute 8.8.8.8 Cisco IOS: show ip route | ping | traceroute Traceroute is the single most useful routing diagnostic tool: by sending packets with incrementing TTLs and observing which hop stops responding, you can pinpoint exactly which router in the path is failing or misrouting traffic — directly exploiting the TTL mechanism described in the Internal Workflow section.
example: Users at a branch office report they can reach internal file servers at headquarters but cannot reach a specific cloud- hosted application. Running `tracert` from an affected workstation shows the path successfully traversing the branch router and the WAN link to headquarters, but stalling at the headquarters edge router — the hop that should be forwarding toward the internet/cloud provider. Checking that router's routing table reveals the default route was accidentally removed during a recent configuration change. Restoring the default route resolves the issue immediately. This is a common real-world pattern: partial connectivity (some destinations reachable, others not) almost always points at a specific missing or incorrect route rather than a general "network down" condition, and traceroute is what narrows it to the exact hop.
cloud: Cloud VPCs/VNets use route tables that are directly conceptually identical to what's covered here: each subnet is associated with a route table listing destination CIDR blocks and targets (an internet gateway, a NAT gateway, a peering connection, a VPN, etc.). A "0.0.0.0/0 → Internet Gateway" entry in an AWS route table is the exact same default-route concept described above, just expressed in cloud-native terms. VPC peering and Transit Gateway/VNet peering are essentially routing between separate cloud networks — the same problem this session solves, at cloud scale, covered fully in Layer 9 (Sessions 123–135).
automation: Routing diagnostics are highly scriptable and pair naturally with your PowerShell learning path — a quick reachability/path script exercises exactly the concepts in this session:

Get-NetRoute | Where DestinationPrefix -eq '0.0.0.0/0' # find the default route Test-NetConnection -ComputerName 8.8.8.8 -TraceRoute # PowerShell's built-in traceroute equivalent On Linux, `ip route` shows the routing table and `mtr` (a combined ping+traceroute tool) is a popular real-time path diagnostic. Once you reach network device automation (Session 108+), the same `show ip route` output can be pulled and diffed across routers on a schedule to detect unexpected routing changes — a genuinely valuable monitoring pattern in real enterprise environments.
career: Routing is one of the two or three most heavily tested topics in CCNA (alongside switching and subnetting) and is a near-guaranteed interview topic for any network or sysadmin-adjacent role — expect scenario questions requiring you to reason through a routing table, not just define terms. Static vs. dynamic routing, and the purpose of a default route, are baseline questions that separate candidates who've only read about networking from those who've actually configured it.

For your Secure Branch Office lab specifically, routing (along with the NAT/PAT you already struggled with) is the connective tissue between subnets — revisiting that lab now, with routing tables in mind, should make the earlier NAT/PAT confusion click into place, since NAT (Session 37) is applied precisely at routing boundaries.

misconceptions: "Routing and switching are basically the same thing." They solve fundamentally different problems:
switching is local delivery via MAC addresses, routing is inter-network delivery via IP addresses — conflating them is one of the most common early-learner mistakes.

"A packet keeps the same Ethernet frame the whole way to its destination." It doesn't — the Ethernet frame is rebuilt at every router hop; only the IP packet (and its TTL) persists end-to-end, as covered in the Internal Workflow section.

"More specific routes are just extra clutter if a default route exists." The opposite is true — longest prefix match means specific routes always take priority over the default route; the default route is only a fallback for what nothing else matches.

"Dynamic routing protocols are always better than static routes." Static routes are simpler, more predictable, and often preferred for small or stable topologies (like a small branch office); dynamic protocols earn their complexity at larger, more redundant scale.
anchors: "Switches deliver within a neighborhood (MAC), routers deliver between cities (IP)."
"The envelope (Ethernet frame) gets thrown away and rewritten at every post office (router); the letter inside (IP packet) stays the same all the way to its destination."
Default route = 0.0.0.0/0 = "anything not matched by anything more specific."
TTL countdown = traceroute's whole trick: each hop that decrements TTL to 0 replies once, revealing the path one hop at a time.

lab: Routing-focused Packet Tracer lab, extending the switching lab from Session 28:

1. Build a topology: 2 PCs on 2 different subnets, each connected to its own switch, both switches connected to a router (router-on-a-stick or two separate router interfaces). Configure IP addressing and a default gateway on each PC.
2. Ping PC-A to PC-B and use Simulation Mode to watch the frame get rebuilt at the router — pause at each stage and note the changing MAC addresses versus the unchanged IP addresses.
3. Check the router's routing table (`show ip route`) and identify the directly connected routes for each subnet.

4. Add a third subnet with its own router and a static route between the two routers; verify end-to-end reachability, then remove the static route and observe the failure — practice explaining what happened using routing table terms.
5. Run `tracert`/`traceroute` from a PC to a destination two hops away and match each line of output to a router in your topology.

6. Revisit your Secure Branch Office lab's routing configuration specifically — identify which routes are directly connected, which (if any) are static, and where NAT was applied relative to the routing boundary.
